# How can a prediction rule be both reliable and easy to read?

::: {.story-lead}
Classifiers and decision trees learn rules from data to predict an outcome.
Over the years, this line of work has asked how much those rules can be
trusted, has used classifiers on real problems, from ports to health care
fraud, and has developed oblique regression trees that try to be both
accurate and easy to read.
:::
:::

::: {.column-margin .glance}
**At a glance**

Period
:   2013 to the present

Threads
:   Reliability of classifiers; classifiers in practice; oblique trees; multivariate regression trees

Selected collaborators
:   Claudio Conversano, Francesco Mola, Andrea Carta, Giulia Contu, Marco
    Ortu. All authors are listed [with each publication](#publications).

Key paper
:   *Computational Statistics* 2025 (open access)

Latest
:   An interpretable ensemble of oblique trees (IFCS 2026)
:::

## The question

Classification and regression trees split the data with simple rules, such as
"income above a threshold", and predict with the average or the most frequent
class of each group. Two questions run through this line of work. How much can
we trust the rule that a classifier has learned from the data at hand? And can
a tree stay easy to read while following the structure of the data?

## A tree for an applied prediction problem [2013–2014]{.period} {#ports}

At a transhipment container terminal, planning each work shift depends on
when ships actually arrive, and the arrival times notified by ship operators
are often revised. After an exploratory analysis of the delays recorded at a
Mediterranean terminal, the article proposed using a classification and
regression tree (CART), an established method, to reduce the uncertainty about
arrivals ({{< cite pani2014data >}}).
A conference paper had compared machine learning methods to predict delays in
container terminals ({{< cite cannas2013delay text="WCTR 2013" >}}).

## How reliable is a classifier? [2014–2019]{.period} {#reliability}

A classifier may perform well on the data at hand and still learn an unstable
rule, especially when classes are imbalanced or observations are few. We
proposed to assess the reliability of a multi-class classifier by retraining
it on resampled versions of the data
({{< cite frigau2014assessing text="ECDA 2014" >}};
{{< cite frigau2016assessing text="Springer, 2016" >}}). User-defined
misclassification costs, applied to the resulting confusion matrices and
modeled with a Beta regression, give a cost-sensitive classification index; a
second index measures how much the distribution of the predicted classes
differs from the observed one. Both lie between 0 and 1, so each classifier
becomes a point in a square, and its position on the original and resampled
data shows how reliable it is.

Other conference contributions of those years dealt with a bivariate
cost-sensitive classifier performance index
({{< cite frigau2014bivariate text="COMPSTAT 2014" >}}), the reliability of a
classifier ({{< cite frigau2015note text="CLADAG 2015" >}}), combined methods
for multi-label classification
({{< cite frigau2017combined text="CLADAG 2017" >}}), the sequential automatic
search of a subset of classifiers, SASSC, also applied to insurance data
({{< cite frigau2017advances text="IFCS 2017" >}};
{{< cite frigau2017sassc text="MIPIS 2017" >}}), and regularization in
tree-based classification models
({{< cite frigau2019regularization text="ISBIS 2019" >}}).

## Classifiers in practice [2021–2023]{.period} {#practice}

Health care fraud detection applies classifiers to large claims data in which
fraud is rare and its distribution skewed. We compared several classification
algorithms and data
pre-processing methods on publicly available claims payment data of U.S.
Medicare Part B, under several fraud scenarios, and discussed their accuracy
and computational demand, to help practitioners choose and apply a method
({{< cite ekin2021health >}}). The data are on [GitHub](../software.qmd).

Supervised learning is useful beyond classification. Near-infrared spectra of
paper books dated between 1851 and 2000, combined with three supervised
machine learning methods, predicted the year of publication: two of the
methods reached an accuracy of up to two years, and the most informative
wavelengths could be linked to the structure of cellulose and of proteins
({{< cite coppola2023near >}}; see also
{{< cite coppola2023machine text="TECHNART 2023" >}}). A conference
contribution used machine learning models to discriminate tourist landscapes
from eye-tracking data ({{< cite zammarchi2021application text="ENBIS 2021" >}}).

## Oblique trees [2025–2026]{.period} {#oblique}

Each rule of a standard tree involves a single variable. When the response
changes along a combination of variables, a tree needs a staircase of splits
to follow it: it becomes deeper, less stable and harder to read. Oblique trees
split on a linear combination of predictors instead: at each node, a
hyperplane rather than a line parallel to one of the axes.

{{< story-figure files="assets/img/stories/oblique-axis.svg,assets/img/stories/oblique-oblique.svg" labels="Splits parallel to the axes|Oblique splits" caption="Schematic illustration with simulated data. The colour of the points is the response, which increases along the diagonal; shaded areas are the regions defined by the splits." >}}

The difficulty is to find good hyperplanes quickly. TORS, which we developed,
does it in three steps at each node ({{< cite carta2025tree >}}):

1. it selects the predictors most correlated with the response;
2. it splits the continuous response into two classes;
3. it uses a weighted support vector machine with a linear kernel to find the
   hyperplane that minimizes the deviance.

We compared TORS with four other oblique trees and a standard regression tree
(CART), using five-fold cross-validation. On 3,840 simulated data sets, TORS
obtained the lowest root mean squared error more often than the other five
models. On 109 real benchmark data sets, it had the lowest error on 52, more
than any other model, and was first or second on about three quarters; its
relative performance was best on the smallest data sets. Because each split
shows which variables it uses, TORS is easier to interpret than oblique trees
that do not select variables. With only the two predictors most correlated with the
response, the setting that gave the best predictions in the simulations, each
split can be drawn in a plane.

{{< result-bars labels="TORS|ODT|CART|HHCART|BUTIA|CO2" values="52|32|15|6|4|0" highlight="TORS" caption="Benchmark data sets, out of 109, on which each model had the lowest root mean squared error in five-fold cross-validation, as marked in Table 3 of the article. CO2 could not be computed on 9 data sets." >}}

WOLTReg, a related method that we proposed, finds the oblique splits with a
weighted logistic regression instead of a support vector machine, again with a
selection of predictors at each node. On benchmark data sets it worked better
when only a few predictors defined each split, and in the comparison reported
in the chapter it had a lower root mean squared error than other oblique trees
and a standard tree ({{< cite carta2025weighted text="Springer, 2025" >}};
{{< cite carta2025weightedb text="CLADAG 2025" >}}).

Further contributions concern feature-selective oblique trees for regression,
applied to the wages of STEM graduates in Italy
({{< cite carta2025feature text="ICSTA 2025" >}}), a new approach to oblique
decision trees for regression ({{< cite carta2026novel text="ISI 2025" >}}),
and an interpretable ensemble of oblique trees based on weighted support
vector machines ({{< cite carta2026interpretable text="IFCS 2026" >}}).

## Multivariate regression trees for territorial data [2023–2026]{.period} {#mrt}

Multivariate regression trees predict several responses at once and group
similar units along the way. They were used to study Italian mortality rates
({{< cite contu2023multivariate text="CLADAG 2023" >}}) and the determinants of
tourist arrivals in the 307 municipalities of Sardinia, with arrivals by
nationality as responses and geography, demographic structure and transport
accessibility as predictors. The density of accommodation facilities emerged
as the main determinant, together with a persistent difference between the
coast and the inland ({{< cite contu2026territorial text="Springer, 2026" >}};
see also {{< cite contu2026multivariate text="IFCS 2026" >}}).
